title: Chlamydia
body:
Chlamydia trachomatis (non-LGV serovars D-K) causes a bacterial infection of the genital tract, and also of the rectum, throat, or eyes depending on exposure. Asymptomatic infection is common, so case-finding depends on screening rather than symptoms alone.

Symptoms and signs: Signs, when present, can include unusual discharge, burning or discomfort when passing urine, pain or discomfort in the lower abdomen or pelvis, and pain during sex. Many infections cause no signs at all.

Testing: Testing is usually a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) on a urine sample or a genital swab, as advised by a clinician. A clinician decides which sites to test based on the kind of sexual contact.

CURE STATUS: Curable. Chlamydia can be cleared with antibiotics prescribed by a clinician. Finishing the prescribed course and returning for any retest the clinician advises are part of the pathway.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for chlamydia. A past infection does not protect against a future one, so prevention and retesting still matter after treatment.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician for testing, take only the antibiotics the clinician prescribes, tell recent sexual partners so they can be tested and treated, avoid sex until the clinician says treatment is complete, and return for the retest the clinician advises.

Partner care: recent sexual partners should be offered testing and treatment, because untreated partners can pass the infection back. A clinician or clinic can help with partner notification.

Prevention: use condoms consistently, test regularly when sexually active with new or multiple partners, and test again after treatment as advised.

Mechanism and terminology: C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium. Untreated infection can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease, which is associated with chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility, which is why screening and partner treatment are standard care.

See a clinician direction: if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed, or you may have been exposed, see a clinician promptly for testing and advice. Do not try to treat this on your own, and do not use leftover medicines or someone else's prescription.

title: Gonorrhea
body:
Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhea at genital, rectal, and pharyngeal sites. Asymptomatic infection is common, and antimicrobial resistance is a watched public-health problem, so treatment choice and test of cure follow current clinical guidance.

Symptoms and signs: Signs, when present, can include unusual discharge, burning when passing urine, soreness, and rectal discomfort or discharge. Throat infection usually causes no signs.

Testing: Testing is usually a NAAT on a urine sample, swab, or site-specific sample, and a clinician may also arrange culture so drug resistance can be checked. A clinician decides which sites to test.

CURE STATUS: Curable. Gonorrhea can be cleared with antibiotics prescribed by a clinician. Drug resistance is watched closely, so follow-up testing after treatment matters and a clinician may change the plan if the first treatment does not clear the infection.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for gonorrhea. A past infection does not protect against a future one.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician for testing, take only the antibiotics the clinician prescribes, return for the follow-up test the clinician advises so any resistant infection is caught, tell recent sexual partners so they can be tested and treated, and avoid sex until the clinician says treatment is complete.

Partner care: recent sexual partners should be offered testing and treatment. Because resistance is possible, partners also need follow-up testing as their clinician advises.

Prevention: use condoms consistently, test regularly when sexually active with new or multiple partners, and test at every exposed site a clinician recommends.

Mechanism and terminology: N. gonorrhoeae is a Gram-negative diplococcus. Resistance to several antibiotic classes has been documented, which is why guidelines, susceptibility testing, and test of cure are part of standard management rather than optional extras.

See a clinician direction: if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed, or you may have been exposed, see a clinician promptly for testing and advice. Do not try to treat this on your own, and do not use leftover medicines or someone else's prescription.

title: Syphilis
body:
Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, a staged infection: primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary stages. Early infection is highly transmissible, and late untreated infection can damage the heart, brain, and other organs, so early serologic diagnosis and treatment are central to control.

Symptoms and signs: Signs can include a painless sore at the site of contact, a rash (often on the palms or soles), fever, swollen glands, and sores in the mouth or genital area. Later stages may cause no signs for years while damage continues.

Testing: Testing is by blood tests (serology) as advised by a clinician, sometimes with direct examination of a sore. A clinician interprets the blood-test pattern to judge the stage and whether treatment has worked.

CURE STATUS: Curable. Syphilis can be cleared with antibiotics prescribed by a clinician, with the regimen chosen by the clinician for the stage of infection. Follow-up blood tests check that treatment has worked.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for syphilis. A past infection does not protect against a future one, and reinfection is possible.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician for blood testing, take only the antibiotics the clinician prescribes for the stage found, attend the follow-up blood tests the clinician schedules, tell recent sexual partners so they can be tested and treated, and avoid sex until the clinician says treatment is complete.

Partner care: recent sexual partners should be offered testing and treatment, and partners in pregnancy need urgent clinician assessment because syphilis can pass to the child.

Prevention: use condoms consistently, test regularly when sexually active with new or multiple partners, and test in pregnancy as clinicians recommend.

Mechanism and terminology: T. pallidum is a spirochete that disseminates widely if untreated. Serologic follow-up uses non-treponemal titres, and a falling titre after treatment is one marker clinicians use to judge response.

See a clinician direction: if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed, or you may have been exposed, see a clinician promptly for testing and advice. Do not try to treat this on your own, and do not use leftover medicines or someone else's prescription.

title: Trichomoniasis
body:
Trichomonas vaginalis, a flagellated protozoan, causes trichomoniasis of the genital tract. Infection is frequently asymptomatic in men and symptomatic in women, and it is associated with increased risk of acquiring other genital infections, which supports routine partner treatment.

Symptoms and signs: Signs, when present, can include unusual discharge, itching or soreness around the genitals, discomfort when passing urine, and discomfort during sex. Many people have no signs.

Testing: Testing is usually a NAAT or microscopy on a genital sample, as advised by a clinician.

CURE STATUS: Curable. Trichomoniasis can be cleared with medicines prescribed by a clinician. Partners are treated at the same time so the infection is not passed back.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for trichomoniasis. A past infection does not protect against a future one.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician for testing, take only the medicines the clinician prescribes, make sure sexual partners are treated as the clinician advises, avoid sex until the clinician says treatment is complete, and return for any retest advised.

Partner care: sexual partners should be offered testing and treatment even if they have no symptoms, because untreated partners can pass the infection back.

Prevention: use condoms consistently and test when symptoms appear or after a partner is diagnosed.

Mechanism and terminology: T. vaginalis adheres to genital mucosal cells and provokes inflammation. Because asymptomatic carriage sustains transmission, concurrent partner therapy is part of standard management.

See a clinician direction: if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed, or you may have been exposed, see a clinician promptly for testing and advice. Do not try to treat this on your own, and do not use leftover medicines or someone else's prescription.

title: Herpes (HSV-1 and HSV-2)
body:
Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 establish latency in sensory nerve ganglia after primary infection, with periodic reactivation producing recurrent lesions. Shedding can occur without visible lesions, which is why transmission can happen between outbreaks.

Symptoms and signs: Signs can include blisters or sores around the mouth or genitals, tingling or itching before an outbreak, and flu-like feelings during a first outbreak. Outbreaks vary in frequency and severity from person to person.

Testing: Testing is usually a swab or laboratory test of a sore during an outbreak, or a blood test as advised by a clinician. A clinician explains what each test can and cannot show.

CURE STATUS: No cure exists for herpes. Antiviral medicines cannot remove the virus from the body, but they can shorten outbreaks and reduce how often outbreaks happen.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for herpes. A past infection does not protect against a future one, and either virus type can be passed on even without visible sores.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician for testing and advice, discuss antiviral medicines the clinician may prescribe to treat outbreaks or to suppress them, learn the early signs of an outbreak, tell sexual partners, and use condoms and avoid contact during outbreaks as the clinician advises.

Partner care: tell sexual partners so they can learn their own status and discuss prevention with a clinician. Suppressive treatment and condom use, as a clinician advises, lower but do not remove the chance of passing the virus on.

Prevention: use condoms consistently, avoid sexual contact during outbreaks and when early warning signs appear, and talk with a clinician about suppressive treatment where appropriate.

Mechanism and terminology: after primary infection, HSV persists latently in sensory ganglia; reactivation travels back along nerves to the skin or mucosa. Antivirals inhibit viral replication during reactivation but do not eliminate latent virus, which is the reason management is suppressive rather than eradicative.

See a clinician direction: if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed, or you may have been exposed, see a clinician promptly for testing and advice. Do not try to treat this on your own, and do not use leftover medicines or someone else's prescription.

title: HIV
body:
HIV targets CD4-bearing cells of the body's defence system, and untreated infection progressively weakens that system. Modern antiretroviral therapy suppresses viral replication, preserves defence function, and prevents onward sexual transmission when suppression is sustained.

Symptoms and signs: Early infection may cause a flu-like illness, but many people have no signs for years. Later untreated infection can cause weight loss, fevers, night sweats, and repeated infections. Only testing can show HIV status.

Testing: Testing is by blood tests, including antigen-antibody tests, as advised by a clinician. Clinics also offer rapid tests, and a clinician confirms any reactive result with follow-up testing.

CURE STATUS: There is no general cure for HIV. Antiretroviral medicines prescribed by a clinician suppress the virus and protect health, but they must be taken as prescribed and do not remove the virus from the body.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for HIV. A past exposure does not protect against infection, and prevention depends on the steps below.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician promptly for testing, start and stay on the antiretroviral treatment the clinician prescribes, attend regular follow-up and laboratory checks, and discuss with a clinician how effective treatment that keeps the virus suppressed means HIV cannot be passed to a sexual partner. People at risk can ask a clinician about pre-exposure prevention medicines, and anyone with a recent possible exposure should seek urgent clinician care about post-exposure options.

Partner care: tell sexual partners so they can be tested and, where appropriate, discuss prevention medicines with a clinician. With sustained viral suppression on treatment, onward sexual transmission does not occur, which clinicians describe as undetectable equals untransmittable.

Prevention: use condoms consistently, test regularly, ask a clinician about pre-exposure prevention medicines if at risk, and seek urgent clinician care after a possible exposure.

Mechanism and terminology: HIV integrates into host-cell DNA as provirus, which is why therapy suppresses replication without eradicating infection. Viral load monitoring guides therapy, and sustained undetectable viral load is the marker associated with non-transmission through sex.

See a clinician direction: if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed, or you may have been exposed, see a clinician promptly for testing and advice. Do not try to treat this on your own, and do not use leftover medicines or someone else's prescription.

title: HPV
body:
Human papillomavirus comprises many genotypes, divided into low-risk types associated with warts and high-risk types associated with cervical and other anogenital cancers. Most infections are transient, while persistent high-risk infection can drive precancerous change over years, which is why screening and vaccination are the control pillars.

Symptoms and signs: Many infections cause no signs. Low-risk types can cause warts on the genitals or around the anus. High-risk types usually cause no signs until cell changes or cancer develop, which is why screening matters.

Testing: Testing depends on the situation: a clinician examines warts directly, and cervical screening programmes use HPV testing and cell examination as local guidelines advise. There is no single general HPV test for everyone, and a clinician explains which test applies.

title: Mycoplasma genitalium
body:
Mycoplasma genitalium is a fastidious bacterium associated with urethritis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance are increasingly documented, so resistance-guided therapy and test of cure are part of current management.

title: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV)
body:
Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by invasive C. trachomatis serovars L1-L3, which spread through lymphatic tissue and produce proctocolitis or inguinal disease. Management uses a longer clinician-directed antibiotic course than non-LGV chlamydia, with follow-up to confirm resolution.

title: Hepatitis C
body:
Hepatitis C virus is a bloodborne flavivirus and a leading cause of chronic liver disease. Sexual transmission occurs, with higher risk where blood exposure is involved, and most acute infections are asymptomatic, so diagnosis usually follows risk-based or routine screening.

Symptoms and signs: Most people have no signs at first. When signs appear they can include tiredness, loss of appetite, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and yellowing of the skin or eyes. Long-term untreated infection can damage the liver over years.

Testing: Testing is by blood tests: an antibody test followed by a test for the virus itself, as a clinician advises. A clinician also checks liver health and whether other infections are present.

CURE STATUS: Curable. Hepatitis C can be cleared with antiviral medicines prescribed by a clinician. Modern antiviral courses clear the virus in most people who complete them as prescribed, and follow-up blood tests confirm the result.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for hepatitis C. Clearing the infection does not protect against a future infection, so prevention still matters after treatment.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician for blood testing and liver assessment, take only the antiviral medicines the clinician prescribes, complete the course, return for the follow-up blood test that confirms clearance, avoid alcohol as the clinician advises, and tell sexual and needle-sharing contacts so they can be tested.

Partner care: sexual partners and anyone who shared blood-exposure risks should be offered testing. Condoms lower sexual transmission risk, and never sharing injecting equipment removes the largest bloodborne risk.

Prevention: use condoms, never share injecting equipment, avoid sharing razors or toothbrushes that may carry blood, and test after any blood exposure.

Mechanism and terminology: HCV replicates in liver cells and establishes chronic infection in most exposed people. Direct-acting antivirals target viral proteins and achieve sustained virologic response, the marker clinicians use to confirm clearance.

See a clinician direction: if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed, or you may have been exposed, see a clinician promptly for testing and advice. Do not try to treat this on your own, and do not use leftover medicines or someone else's prescription.

title: Hepatitis B
body:
Hepatitis B virus is a partially double-stranded DNA virus transmitted sexually, through blood, and perinatally. Acute adult infection usually resolves, while infection acquired early in life commonly becomes chronic, with long-term risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer, which is why vaccination and screening are central.

Symptoms and signs: Many people have no signs. When signs appear they can include tiredness, loss of appetite, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and yellowing of the skin or eyes. Chronic infection often causes no signs until liver damage is advanced.

Testing: Testing is by blood tests that show whether infection is new, long-term, or past, and whether vaccination has been given, as a clinician advises. Household and sexual contacts are also offered testing and vaccination advice.

CURE STATUS: There is no general cure for chronic hepatitis B. Antiviral medicines prescribed by a clinician can suppress the virus and protect the liver, and acute infections in adults usually clear with supportive clinician care, but long-term infection is managed rather than removed.

IMMUNITY STATUS: Vaccine-induced protection exists for hepatitis B. Vaccination can protect against new infection, and it is recommended for people at risk and for infants. Household and sexual contacts of a person with hepatitis B should ask a clinician about vaccination and testing.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician for blood testing and liver assessment, take only the antiviral medicines the clinician prescribes if treatment is advised, attend regular liver monitoring, avoid alcohol as the clinician advises, and make sure household and sexual contacts are offered testing and vaccination advice.

Partner care: sexual partners and household contacts should be tested and offered vaccination as a clinician advises, and condoms lower transmission risk until a partner's protection is confirmed by a clinician.

Prevention: vaccination is the strongest protection, condoms lower sexual risk, never share injecting equipment, and test in pregnancy so newborn protection can be arranged.

Mechanism and terminology: HBV persists in liver cells as covalently closed circular DNA, which is why suppression rather than eradication is the usual therapeutic goal, and why serologic markers distinguish infection, past infection, and vaccine-derived protection.

title: Pubic lice
body:
Pthirus pubis infests coarse hair, principally pubic hair, with transmission by close contact. Diagnosis is by visual identification of lice or nits, and treatment combines topical therapy with environmental measures and partner treatment.

Symptoms and signs: Signs can include itching in the affected area, small spots of blood or irritation on skin or underwear, and visible tiny insects or eggs attached to hairs.

Testing: Testing is by visual examination, as a clinician or pharmacist advises. A clinician may also check for other infections passed through sexual contact.

CURE STATUS: Curable in the treatment sense. The infestation can be cleared with treatment recommended by a clinician or pharmacist, together with washing bedding and clothing and treating sexual partners.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for pubic lice. A past infestation does not protect against a future one.

title: Scabies
body:
Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis burrows in the stratum corneum, and the host response to mites, eggs, and waste produces intense pruritus, characteristically worse at night, with burrows and papules in characteristic distributions.

Symptoms and signs: Signs can include intense itching, especially at night, thin burrow lines on the skin, and a rash of small bumps, often between the fingers, on the wrists, waistline, and genitals.

title: Molluscum contagiosum
body:
Molluscum contagiosum virus, a poxvirus, produces umbilicated papules by skin-to-skin transmission, including sexual transmission in adults. Infection is usually self-limited, and management balances lesion treatment against the natural course and the risk of scarring.

Symptoms and signs: Signs are smooth, firm, round bumps on the skin, often with a small dimple in the centre. They are usually painless, though scratching can make them sore or infected.

Testing: Testing is by skin examination, as a clinician advises. Laboratory testing is rarely needed.

CURE STATUS: Not curable with antibiotics, because this is a viral skin condition rather than a bacterial infection. Lesions are treatable: a clinician may remove them or advise watchful waiting while they clear over time, and new bumps can appear during that period.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for molluscum contagiosum. A past episode does not reliably protect against a future one.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician for examination, follow the clinician's choice between lesion treatment and watchful waiting, avoid scratching and shaving over bumps, cover bumps during close contact as advised, and tell sexual partners so they can be examined.

Partner care: sexual partners should be examined as the clinician advises, and contact over affected skin should be avoided until a clinician says otherwise.

Prevention: avoid skin-to-skin contact with affected skin, do not share towels or razors, and avoid scratching, which spreads bumps to nearby skin.

Mechanism and terminology: the virus replicates in epidermal cells and evades local responses for months, so lesions persist and then resolve as the body's response catches up, which is why watchful waiting is a legitimate clinician option.

See a clinician direction: if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed, or you may have been exposed, see a clinician promptly for testing and advice. Do not try to treat this on your own, and do not use leftover medicines or someone else's prescription.

title: Bacterial vaginosis (associated condition)
category: Associated condition, not strictly an STD
body:
Bacterial vaginosis is a dysbiosis of the vaginal microbiota, marked by loss of lactobacilli and overgrowth of mixed anaerobes. It is classified as an associated condition rather than a classic sexually transmitted infection, though sexual activity is epidemiologically associated, and it is included here with that distinction explicit.

Symptoms and signs: Signs can include unusual discharge, often thin and greyish, and an unpleasant odour, sometimes stronger after sex. Some people have no signs. Itching and soreness are less typical and should prompt clinician assessment for other causes.

Testing: Testing is by clinical examination and laboratory checks on a vaginal sample, as a clinician advises, including pH and microscopy findings.

CURE STATUS: Not described as a single cure, because bacterial vaginosis is a balance problem rather than one invading germ. It is manageable: treatment prescribed by a clinician usually settles an episode, but recurrence is common and repeat clinician care is often needed.

IMMUNITY STATUS: No vaccine exists for bacterial vaginosis. A past episode does not protect against a future one, and recurrence is common.

WAYS TO FIX: See a clinician for examination and testing, take only the treatment the clinician prescribes, return if symptoms come back, avoid douching and scented products as the clinician advises, and discuss with a clinician whether partner treatment is relevant in your situation.

Partner care: routine partner treatment is not the standard fix for bacterial vaginosis, so a clinician advises what, if anything, a partner should do. Partners should still be offered testing for other infections where relevant.

Prevention: avoid douching, use condoms, limit scented products around the genitals, and seek clinician care promptly when symptoms return rather than repeating old treatment on your own.

Mechanism and terminology: the condition reflects a shift from lactobacillus-dominant flora to a polymicrobial anaerobic community with raised pH and clue cells on microscopy. Recurrence reflects re-establishment of that community, not failure of a single drug.

See a clinician direction: if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed, or you may have been exposed, see a clinician promptly for testing and advice. Do not try to treat this on your own, and do not use leftover medicines or someone else's prescription.
